title: Phishing the THAAD contractors
review_note: Rewritten in plain language. Core facts re-checked Oct 2026 against the DOJ release, Newsweek, SecurityWeek, PBS/AP and CyberScoop. The full complaint PDF was not read directly; affidavit details come from partial OCR and press coverage of it.

scenes.label: A job offer that looked too good
scenes.narration: [dramatically] North Korean hackers sent fake job offers to the people building America's missile shield. [short pause] At least, that's what the FBI says. [softly] Here's how it began. It's 2016. An email lands in the inbox of a worker at an American defense company. It's from a recruiter at a rival company. There's a great new job on offer. Some of these emails even mention THAAD. That's the missile shield. [serious] But the recruiter wasn't real. The email was bait. And the US government says the trail led back to North Korea's military.

scenes.label: The shield that stops missiles
scenes.narration: [calmly] So what is THAAD? It's a system that shoots down enemy missiles. It hits them high in the sky, as they fall toward their target. The company in charge of building it is Lockheed Martin. It's one of the biggest weapons makers in America. The plan was to set it up in South Korea. Right next door, North Korea kept testing missiles. [short pause] So the people who built it knew things other countries badly wanted to know.

visuals.query: THAAD interceptor launch Missile Defense Agency

visuals.at: set it up in South Korea

scenes.label: Coders in a Chinese port city
scenes.narration: Meanwhile, across the sea, there's a busy port city in China called Dalian. It's not far from North Korea. Here, a team of North Korean programmers worked for a company called Chosun Expo. They took paid coding jobs for outside customers. One of them was a man named Park Jin Hyok. Investigators say he worked for this company for more than ten years. [cautiously] On paper, it was a normal tech business. But the US government says it was a front. A cover, tied to a North Korean military spy unit called Lab 110.

visuals.at: a team of North Korean programmers
a man named Park Jin Hyok
a North Korean military spy unit

scenes.label: A crew with a long record
scenes.narration: Security experts had a nickname for this hacking crew. They called it the Lazarus Group. By 2016, the US says, it already had a long record. In November 2014, it hacked Sony Pictures. That was payback for a comedy movie that made fun of North Korea's leader. Then, in February 2016, it stole $81 million from Bangladesh's central bank. [pause] Now, according to prosecutors, the same crew picked a new kind of target. Not a movie studio. Not a bank. America's defense companies.

scenes.label: Doing their homework first
scenes.narration: [cautiously] Before you trick someone, you need to know them. And the FBI says these hackers did their homework. Records show someone using a North Korean internet address. They visited the websites of targets like Lockheed Martin. At the same time, they were looking up Lockheed workers. And they were sending messages to its employees. Reports on the case say this was their habit. Before their attacks that worked, they studied their targets online. They checked social media, too. [short pause] Then they set the bait.

scenes.label: The recruiter who didn't exist
scenes.narration: The bait was a trick called spear-phishing. Normal phishing is like a big fishing net. The same scam email goes out to thousands of people. Spear-phishing is aimed at just one person. It's personal. It looks real. It's built to make you click a link or open a file. Here's how it worked this time, investigators say. The hackers made email accounts in the names of recruiters at one defense company. Then they wrote to workers at rival companies. [softly] Think about it. A job offer feels flattering. It feels private. It's just the kind of email you want to open.

scenes.label: THAAD named in the bait
scenes.narration: Some of these emails, the Justice Department says, mentioned THAAD by name. [serious] Then, in May 2017, the shield was set up in South Korea. Tension with North Korea was rising fast. That summer, a security company called Palo Alto Networks spotted something. It found emails full of hidden malware, dressed up as job ads. Malware just means harmful software. The emails went to people who worked for US military contractors. Researchers linked them to the Lazarus Group. One fake ad, Newsweek reported, was for a manager job on the THAAD program.

scenes.label: Fireworks and missiles
scenes.narration: The timing was hard to ignore. On July 4, 2017, America's Independence Day, North Korea launched a missile. It was a new kind, called the Hwasong-14. It was built to fly from one continent to another. On July 28, North Korea launched another one. Newsweek reported the test showed its missiles might reach the western United States. [pause] And right around then, those fake job ads were landing in inboxes. [short pause] So did anyone fall for it?

scenes.label: The door that held
scenes.narration: [surprised] At Lockheed Martin, the answer was no. The Justice Department says the attempts to break into Lockheed's computers did not succeed. [exhales] In hacking stories, that's a rare happy ending. But there's a lot we still don't know. The government hasn't said what stopped them. It hasn't said how many emails went out. And it hasn't said if every other company was as lucky. [serious] The hackers had failed here. But they had left something behind.

visuals.at: a lot we still don't know

scenes.label: One hundred search warrants
scenes.narration: In Los Angeles, FBI agents had been chasing this crew since the Sony hack in 2014. The case grew and grew. In the end, agents used about 100 search warrants. That let them look inside roughly 1,000 email and social media accounts. [cautiously] And they found clues tying the job-offer emails back to Sony. Some used the same fake names and accounts as the Sony attack. Some were opened from North Korean internet addresses. The hacking tools even shared a rare building block with the Sony tools. Different target. Same crew.

scenes.label: The fake name that slipped
scenes.narration: Then the hackers' cover started to slip. They used a fake name online: Kim Hyon Woo. That name was on several email and social media accounts. Park, meanwhile, had his own real accounts for his normal job. Investigators say the two worlds touched. Both email names started with the same three letters, tty. Each account was saved in the other's address book. And both were reached from some of the same internet addresses. [short pause] It was like two strangers who kept using the same front door.

visuals.at: several email and social media accounts

scenes.label: A résumé and a lack of opsec
scenes.narration: Then agents found Park's résumé. It said he worked as a developer. One of his skills was a coding language called Visual C++. Agents say that's the language used to build many of the Lazarus Group's hacking tools. [sarcastic] For a man accused of hiding behind fake names, he left a very real paper trail. Eric Chien, an expert at the security company Symantec, called it "a lack of opsec." Opsec means keeping your secret work apart from your real life. [short pause] Park, the FBI says, didn't.

visuals.at: many of the Lazarus Group's hacking tools

scenes.label: Charged, but out of reach
scenes.narration: On June 8, 2018, prosecutors in Los Angeles filed charges in secret. On September 6, they made them public. Park Jin Hyok was charged with two crimes: hacking and fraud. The most serious one carries up to 20 years in prison. The case also tied the crew to WannaCry, a 2017 attack that locked up computers around the world. The Treasury also hit Park with sanctions. [serious] FBI Director Christopher Wray said: "We stand with our partners to name the North Korean government as the force behind this destructive global cyber campaign."

scenes.label: The job offer that never stopped
scenes.narration: Park has never been arrested. The US and North Korea have no deal to hand over suspects. So he's on the FBI's Most Wanted list, far out of reach. North Korea says it wasn't involved. [reflective] And the trick he's accused of helping run never really went away. In 2020, researchers at McAfee reported more fake job offers. They believed North Korean hackers were behind them. This time they went after defense and aerospace workers. [softly] So the next time a stranger offers you a dream job… read it twice. [short pause] If you like true stories like this, subscribe to Breach Uncovered.

visuals.at: no deal to hand over suspects

facts.claim: In 2016-2017 the conspiracy sent spear-phishing emails to US defense contractors including Lockheed Martin, prime contractor for THAAD; some emails purported to be from recruiters at competing contractors and some referenced THAAD, deployed in South Korea
Attempts to breach Lockheed Martin were unsuccessful
Park Jin Hyok worked for over a decade for Chosun Expo Joint Venture, affiliated with Lab 110, a component of North Korean military intelligence; researchers call the team Lazarus Group
Park worked among a team of North Korean programmers employed by Chosun Expo in Dalian, China, on paid programming/IT projects
Subjects using North Korean IP Address #6 visited websites of intended victims such as Lockheed Martin while researching Lockheed personnel and messaging employees
Subjects created accounts in names of recruiters or high-profile personnel at one company to send recruitment messages to employees of competitors such as other defense contractors
Defense-contractor emails used aliases/accounts seen in the Sony attack, sometimes accessed from North Korean IPs, and malware with the same distinct data table as Sony and bank malware
Successful attacks were preceded by reconnaissance of targets online and in social media, including Lockheed Martin employees

In July 2017 Palo Alto Networks reported Lazarus-linked malicious job-ad lures targeting US military contractor employees; one fake ad was for a management position involving THAAD; North Korean missile tests on July 4 and July 28; Hwasong-14 ICBM; THAAD deployed in South Korea May 2017
Investigators filed 100 search warrants covering about 1,000 email and social media accounts; affidavit 179 pages by FBI Special Agent Nathan P. Shields, Los Angeles
Kim Hyon Woo persona linked to Park via shared 'tty' account names, address-book entry, archive access, and common IP addresses; resume listed developer work and Visual C++
Eric Chien of Symantec described Park's account reuse as 'a lack of opsec'; complaint filed June 8, 2018

Charges unsealed September 6, 2018: conspiracy to commit computer fraud and abuse (max 5 years) and conspiracy to commit wire fraud (max 20 years); OFAC sanctioned Park and KEJV; Wray quote; WannaCry hit hundreds of thousands of computers and the UK NHS
US and North Korea have no extradition agreement
Park is on the FBI Most Wanted list
North Korea denied involvement; incident categorized as espionage against Lockheed Martin
North Korean hackers continued using fake job-recruitment emails against aerospace and defense workers (2020)

Park worked at KEJV's offices in Dalian, Liaoning, China; shared 'tty' account names, address-book entries, archive access and common IP addresses linked the Kim Hyon Woo persona to Park; resume listed Visual C++, the language used to create many Lazarus tools
Complaint filed under seal June 8, 2018 in Los Angeles and unsealed September 6, 2018
Defense-contractor spear-phishing used the same aliases and accounts as the Sony attack; John Demers called it one of the most complex and longest cyber investigations the department has taken
In July 2020 McAfee reported suspected North Korean hackers posing as job recruiters to target aerospace and defense workers

seo.youtube_title: How North Korea Tried to Hack America's Missile Shield (THAAD)
seo.youtube_description:
How North Korea tried to hack the company behind THAAD, America's missile shield, using fake job offers from recruiters who didn't exist. The true story of the Lazarus Group, Lockheed Martin and one man the FBI says left a very real paper trail.

In 2016 and 2017, the US Justice Department says, North Korean hackers sent fake recruiting emails to workers at American defense companies, including Lockheed Martin, the main builder of the THAAD missile defense system. Some of the emails even mentioned THAAD by name. The hackers studied their targets online first. But at Lockheed Martin, the break-in attempts failed.

FBI agents in Los Angeles used about 100 search warrants to dig through roughly 1,000 accounts. The clues led to Park Jin Hyok, a North Korean programmer who worked for a front company in Dalian, China. A fake name, shared accounts and a real résumé helped tie him to the same crew blamed for the Sony Pictures hack and the $81 million Bangladesh Bank heist. He was charged in September 2018. He has never been arrested.
